column11: the US National Epidermolysis Bullosa Registry's dystrophic EB incidence of 6.65 per 1 million live births, on the current US birth count. (1) THE RATE: Eichstadt S, Tang JY, Solis DC, Siprashvili Z, Marinkovich MP, Whitehead N, Schu M, Fang F, Erickson SW, Ritchey ME, Lane AT, 'From Clinical Phenotype to Genotypic Modelling: Incidence and Prevalence of Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB)', Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol 2019;12:933-942, doi 10.2147/CCID.S232547, PMID 31920360, PMC6935313, read 2026-11-16. Table 1, 'Reported Incidence and Prevalence of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa', United States rows attributed to the registry (its reference 14): DEB All 6.65, DDEB All 2.12, RDEB All 3.05, DEB unknown mode 1.48, under the footnote 'Per 1 million live births'. The cells are arithmetically coherent, 2.12 + 3.05 + 1.48 = 6.65. The registry's own paper is Fine JD, 'Epidemiology of Inherited Epidermolysis Bullosa Based on Incidence and Prevalence Estimates From the National Epidermolysis Bullosa Registry', JAMA Dermatol 2016;152(11):1231-1238, doi 10.1001/jamadermatol.2016.2473, PMID 27463098, whose abstract gives only the all-EB figures (19.57 per 1 million live births) and whose subtype table is behind a paywall, which is why the free paper that reproduces it is cited. The RDEB cell is independently corroborated in Tang JY, Marinkovich MP, Lucas E et al., Orphanet J Rare Dis 2021, PMC8045359: 'reported RDEB incidence of 3.05 cases per one million live births'. (2) THE DENOMINATOR: 3,628,934 US births, CDC/NCHS FastStats Births, data year 2024, the page's own stated source 'Births: Final Data for 2024, tables A, C, and 1' (cdc.gov/nchs/fastats/births.htm, read 2026-11-16). (3) 6.65e-6 x 3,628,934 = 24.13
column12: ALL DYSTROPHIC EB, WHICH IS THE POOL THE PREVALENCE ROW ABOVE DESCRIBES; eligible_pct of 0.25 carries the ocular narrowing on top. IT IS INCONSISTENT WITH THAT PREVALENCE BY A KNOWN FACTOR AND THE DIRECTION IS CERTAIN. 3,000 prevalent against 24 a year implies 125 years in the pool, which is true of nobody. The registry is internally coherent - its own prevalence cell of 3.26 per million people, on the US population of 340,110,988 (Census Vintage 2024, nc-est2024-agesex-res.csv), is 1,109 prevalent, a 46-year duration - but the book's prevalence row is not the registry's, it is Krystal's 3,000 from the FY2025 10-K, 2.71 times higher. The registry enrolled voluntarily and closed in 2002. Krystal's own filing carries no incidence: searched in full (0001711279-26-000016), the word appears once, in boilerplate with no number. CONSEQUENCE: built on a scratch copy of the book this layer peaks at 86.8mm USD in year five and then DECLINES (9.3, 25.3, 49.9, 74.4, 86.8, 85.4, 75.7, 63.3) because 24 new DEB patients a year, 6 of them ocular, cannot replace the stock leaving at this asset's stopping rate. For a congenital disease with stable prevalence that decline is an artefact of the low inflow, so the row errs LOW. THE REPLACEMENT if the two sources are ever reconciled: 24.13 x (3,000 / 1,109) = 65 a year, which assumes the registry's under-ascertainment is the same in both cells. That is a derivation, not a source, which is why it is not this row
